title: Bet Hebrew Letter (ב): Sound & Dagesh
description: Learn the Hebrew letter Bet (ב): how the dagesh dot changes its sound between [b] and [v], with beginner explanations, example words and interactive practice.

editorialIssues.detail: Some mark-recognition distractors use letters not introduced in this lesson. Beginner scaffolding can be improved separately from the approved source synchronization.

4.label: Bet with Dagesh
4.equivalent: Bet with a dot (dagesh) in its center, pronounced [b].

blocks.0: Bet Hebrew Letter (ב): Dagesh, Sound & Practice
blocks.3: In modern Hebrew, three letters — Bet, Kaf and Pe — can be pronounced in two different ways, depending on whether they contain a small dot called a "dagesh." One of them is Bet (בּ).
blocks.7: At the start of a word, Bet has a dagesh and is pronounced [b]. When a prefix such as ו (and) is attached, it can change to [v], as in וּבָנִים [u-vanim].
blocks.13: The Hebrew word 'אַבָּא' [aba] means "father." It consists of Aleph (א), Bet (בּ), and another Aleph (א). A patach (ַ) under the first Aleph gives the [a] sound, and a dagesh with a kamatz (ָ) under the Bet produce [ba]. The final Aleph is silent.
blocks.15: The Hebrew word 'בָּא' [ba] consists of Bet (בּ) and Aleph (א). The Bet has a dagesh, indicating a strong [b] sound. A kamatz (ָ) beneath it gives the [ba] sound. The Aleph does not have a vowel and remains silent.

6.content: When the letter Bet (ב) appears at the beginning of a word, does it usually have a dot (Dagesh) and sound like [b]?
6.tip: In most cases, Bet at the beginning of a word has a Dagesh inside and is pronounced like [b]. However, exceptions exist in certain grammatical contexts — for example, when a prefix such as ו (and) is attached, as in וּבָנִים [u-vanim].

8.content: At the end of a word, Bet usually sounds like [b].
8.tip: Word-final Bet is almost always pronounced [v], as in לֵב [lev].

10.tip: The vowel sign with a horizontal line and two dots beside it is called 'Hataf Patah.' It represents a reduced [a] sound.

12.tip: Dagesh in Bet produces a plosive [b] sound, while without it, Bet sounds like [v]. Patah and Kamatz Gadol both give the [a] sound, and Hataf Patah is a reduced [a].

theory.heading: Meet Bet
theory.intro: The second letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Bet is one of a few letters that can make two different sounds.
objectives: Tell Bet with a dagesh (<bdi class="hebrew" lang="he" dir="rtl">בּ</bdi>, [b]) apart from Bet without one (<bdi class="hebrew" lang="he" dir="rtl">ב</bdi>, [v]).
Read the dagesh in real words like <bdi class="hebrew" lang="he" dir="rtl">אַבָּא</bdi> (father).

examples.heading: Bet with and without the dagesh
examples.intro: Compare Bet with the dagesh dot and without it, then see both forms in real Hebrew words.
